input.raw_text: We woke up to a different country. Sterling is down eight big figures, trading at levels not seen since the mid-eighties, and the board is a mess — every time a count comes in from a Leave area the pound ticks lower. European bank shares are in freefall: RBS is down more than a third, Barclays isn't much better, and the Italian and Spanish banks are limit-down. The FTSE opened about eight percent lower and has clawed back half of that, which tells you equities at least see this as a sterling and bank problem first. Gold is up better than a hundred dollars. Carney has been on the wires promising £250 billion of support if needed, and that has steadied rates somewhat. A vote that was supposed to be a coin flip is being traded as a regime change.
input.summary: Sterling fell sharply to levels last seen in the mid-1980s as referendum results favored Leave, while European bank shares suffered severe losses, UK equities partially recovered from an eight-percent opening decline, gold rose by more than one hundred dollars, and announced central-bank support helped steady rates amid broad repricing toward regime-change uncertainty.

interpretation.summary: The packet weakly supports three bear-stress states through concurrent European bank losses and a sharp, volatile UK equity decline, while model-derived correlations, factor shares, and filtered regime probabilities remain unavailable.

citations.text: The share of total return variance explained by the first principal component (PC1) across U.S. financial sector monthly returns (banks, broker-dealers, insurers, hedge funds). PC1 variance share of approximately 77% signals the baseline systemic co-movement regime (1994-2000); values rising toward or above 80% signal elevated interconnectedness (2001-2008 average: 83%). The cross-sector PC1 factor loading differential—broker-dealers loading at 0.79 vs. hedge funds at 0.13—identifies broker-dealers as the dominant systemic node. PC1 is computable from rolling PCA on monthly sector return series. Values above 90% indicate extreme stress events (e.g., August 1998 LTCM: 93%). pc1_variance_share; broker_dealer_pc1_loading; hedge_fund_pc1_loading; rolling_pca_window PC1 share thresholds: baseline ~77%, elevated ~83%, extreme stress >90%. Broker-dealer PC1 loading (0.79) vs. hedge fund (0.13) is a structural cross-sector signature; the contrast reflects balance sheet leverage exposure vs. strategy idiosyncrasy. Applicable to rolling window monitoring of systemic interconnectedness in financial sector return data.

matched_states.state_summary: A market condition in which the returns of major financial sector institutions (banks, broker-dealers, insurers, and hedge funds) are driven predominantly by a single common factor, as measured by the first principal component (PC1) explaining a high share of cross-sector return variance. During normal periods PC1 explains approximately 77% of variance (1994-2000); during crisis periods it rises to 83% on average (2001-2008) and peaks at 93% (August 1998, LTCM crisis) and exceeds 80% throughout the 2007-2009 financial crisis. Broker- dealers load heavily on PC1 (loading=0.79) indicating they are the primary drivers of systemic common variation, while hedge funds load weakly (0.13). The state reflects collapsed cross-sector diversification and concentrated systemic exposure. Estimated on U.S. monthly financial sector returns 1994-2008 (Billio et al. 2012).
matched_states.title: Financial Sector Systemic Co-movement State

citations.text: A two-regime Markov-switching model identifies a normal regime (monthly mean μ=0.90%, volatility σ=2.81%) and a bear regime (monthly mean μ=0.13%, volatility σ=5.04%) in international equity returns. The bear regime exhibits approximately 80% higher volatility and near-zero mean returns compared to the normal regime. Tables 2 and 3, p.5-6. Estimated on world equity index data at monthly frequency. Normal regime corresponds to typical equity conditions; bear regime captures high-volatility drawdown periods. Transition probabilities govern regime persistence.

matched_states.state_summary: A two-state Markov-switching market condition for international equity returns characterized by empirically estimated regime-level parameters: normal regime (monthly mean μ=0.90%, volatility σ=2.81%) and bear regime (monthly mean μ=0.13%, volatility σ=5.04%). The bear regime exhibits approximately 80% higher volatility and near-zero mean returns relative to the normal regime. Transition probabilities govern regime persistence; the Hamilton filter provides real-time probability estimates of the active regime. Estimated on world equity index data at monthly frequency (Ang and Bekaert 2004, Tables 2-3).

citations.text: International equity return correlations approximately 20 percentage points higher during identified bear regime periods versus normal regime periods. Measured as the difference in regime-conditional correlation estimates from a two-state Markov-switching model: corr_bear - corr_normal ≈ +0.20. Observable in rolling correlation estimates that co-move with the Hamilton filter's bear-regime probability: when bear probability is high, realized rolling correlations across international equity pairs are systematically elevated. This pattern confirms diversification benefit collapse during downturns. regime_conditional_correlation_bear; regime_conditional_correlation_normal; bear_minus_normal_correlation_diff; rolling_correlation_vs_regime_probability Empirically documented in Ang-Bekaert (2004) Tables 2-3. The ~20pp correlation differential is the key observable linking regime identification to portfolio diversification failure. Rolling 12-month international equity correlations serve as a real-time proxy observable for this signature.

matched_states.state_summary: A market condition in which international equity return correlations are approximately 20 percentage points higher during the bear regime than during the normal regime. The elevated correlation reduces diversification benefits precisely when they are most needed—during market downturns. This regime-conditional correlation asymmetry is identified by a two-state Markov-switching model on world equity index data (Ang and Bekaert 2004, Tables 2-3). The state is active whenever the filtered bear-regime probability is elevated.
